    Five revolutions in one Tokyo day

    A wall, a station, a bridge, a car plant and a parts market, with an hour's rest at noon.

    This is the Thursday plan. One striking site for each of the first five revolutions, back at the flat to rest from noon to one, home by five. It follows Gemini Deep Research's report of 1 November 2026, checked against the operators' own pages the same day; two train legs were corrected. The longer background version with more sites is the six-revolutions page; stage 6 is the Todai tour. Each fact carries one of three notes: from Gemini, checked means Gemini gave it and an operator's page confirmed it; checked here means it was checked on the operator's page alone; not checked or estimate means nobody confirmed it.

    The day, Thursday

    08:00Leave the flat. Walk east to Naka-Okachimachi station on the Hibiya line, about 7 minutes. estimate
    08:10

    Train 1. Hibiya line, Naka-Okachimachi to Minami-Senju, 4 stops, no change, about 9 minutes. Then walk north-west about 11 minutes, past Minami-Senju 6-chōme, to the wall. estimate Directions

    08:30Stage 1, the Senju wool-mill wall (30 minutes). Walk the long red-brick wall beside Arakawa Technical High School, with its bricked-up gate. Across the street stand Inoue Seizō's bust of 1936, with stone sheep, and the stele his workers raised in 1888; one block east, two panels of the main-gate wall survive by the Life supermarket bicycle park. from Gemini, checked
    09:00

    Train 2. Walk back to JR Minami-Senju (about 10 minutes). Jōban line train that runs on through the Ueno-Tokyo line to Shimbashi, no change, about 20 minutes; then 5 minutes from the Shiodome exit side. If the next train ends at Ueno, take the Hibiya line instead, Minami-Senju to Ginza without a change, and walk 10 minutes. estimate Directions

    09:40Stage 2, Old Shimbashi Station (35 minutes). Walk round the stone-faced station house, rebuilt full size on the 1872 foundations, and the stretch of stone platform with rails behind it. The hall opens at 10:00: fifteen minutes inside for the excavated platform and the models. from Gemini, checked
    10:15

    Walk 1.3 km south-east along Harumi-dōri through Tsukiji, about 20 minutes. estimate Directions

    10:35Stage 3, Kachidoki Bridge and its museum (35 minutes). Walk out over the Sumida on the 1940 riveted steel bridge whose two middle leaves once lifted for ships. Then go into the old substation at the Tsukiji end, where the motors and switchboards that raised the leaves still stand. checked here
    11:15Lunch, Tsukiji outer market (25 minutes). Kitsuneya きつねや, a stall at Tsukiji 4-9-12 that has stood since 1947. Order the beef bowl or the beef and tofu; its famous dish is stewed offal, which is chewy. Open 06:30 to 13:30, or until the rice runs out. from listings Sources disagree on its closing days, so have a second stall in mind. not checked
    11:45

    Train 3. Walk to Tsukiji station, exit 1 (about 4 minutes). Hibiya line, Tsukiji to Naka-Okachimachi, no change, about 12 minutes; then 7 minutes' walk to the flat. estimate Directions

    12:05Rest at the flat, until 13:00.
    13:00

    Train 4. Walk to JR Okachimachi (about 5 minutes). Yamanote line one stop to Akihabara, then change to the Keihin-Tōhoku line southbound, direct to Shin-Koyasu, about 45 minutes. At midday the Keihin-Tōhoku runs fast and skips Okachimachi, which is why you change at Akihabara. estimate Directions

    13:55

    Bus or walk. City bus 19 from the stop in front of Shin-Koyasu station to Takarachō, then 1 minute on; or walk about 17 minutes along the Sangyō-dōri. checked here Bus times not checked Directions

    14:15Stage 4, Nissan's 1935 building (45 minutes). The company's first head office stands among working engine shops, a pale concrete block from the year mass production began here. Downstairs an early Datsun; upstairs a gallery of full-size engines from the 1930s on. checked here
    15:00

    Train 5. Bus or walk back to Shin-Koyasu. Keihin-Tōhoku line northbound, direct to Akihabara, no change, about 45 minutes. estimate Directions

    16:05Stage 5, Akihabara (45 minutes). Step out of the Electric Town exit into the warren of tiny stalls under the railway viaduct, with chips, valves and test meters stacked to the ceiling. Then walk up Chūō-dōri, where the radio-parts market grew into tower blocks of electronics. from Gemini, checked
    16:50

    Walk home, about 1.2 km north past Suehirochō, about 15 minutes; or the Ginza line one stop, Suehirochō to Ueno-hirokōji. estimate Directions

    EveningA quick dinner. Two old houses where one person eats well in half an hour. See below.

    A quick dinner on Thursday

    Hōraiya 蓬莱屋, fillet pork cutlet. Founded in 1912 and at this address, Ueno 3-28-5, since 1928. It is credited with inventing the fillet cutlet, and the film director Ozu Yasujirō ate here. It lies on the walk home from Akihabara, by Okachimachi. Most listings give evenings as 17:00 to 20:00, last order 19:30; one says there is no weekday evening service. Closed Wednesdays. About ¥3,300. No bookings. from listings, which disagree

    Kanda Matsuya 神田まつや, buckwheat noodles. Founded in 1884, in a wooden building that Tokyo lists as historic. One minute from Awajichō station, about eight minutes on foot south-west of Akihabara. Weekdays to 20:00 or 20:30, last order half an hour before; closed Sundays. Noodles with duck are about ¥1,650. from listings Walking time estimate

    Both are old Tokyo houses with plain cooked food and quick service. Neither is a long sitting.

    On foot: about 11.5 km if you walk every leg, counting the map distance plus a quarter for street corners. That is far more than Gemini's 5.8 km and more than the 7 km asked for. Taking bus 19 both ways at Nissan saves about 2.7 km, which brings the day to about 8.5 km. The rest is mostly the walks between stations and sites, which no train shortens. Trains and buses: about 2 hours 20 minutes. All five sites are free. Fares were not checked; Suica covers every leg. estimate

    The five sites

    Stage 1 · Cotton and the factory

    Perez: Arkwright's Cromford mill, 1771  ·  Japan: the Tomioka silk mill, 1872; the army's Senju wool mill, 1879; Kanegafuchi Spinning's Tokyo mill, 1887–89

    Former Senju wool-mill brick wall (旧千住製絨所煉瓦塀), Minami-Senju 6-42 and 6-43, Arakawa ward. Nearest station Minami-Senju (Hibiya line or JR), about 11 minutes on foot.

    Street wall, open at any hour, free. Arakawa ward lists it as a surviving part of the mill (page of 29 Feb 2024). The wall was fenced for inspection and repair in late 2023 and was standing again, repaired, by March 2024.

    The state built this mill in 1879 to clothe its new army in home-made wool instead of imported cloth, behind a European factory wall.

    Stage 2 · Steam and railways

    Perez: Stephenson's Rocket, 1829  ·  Japan: Shimbashi to Yokohama, opened 14 October 1872

    Old Shimbashi Station (旧新橋停車場), Higashi-Shimbashi 1-5-3, Minato ward. Nearest station JR Shimbashi (Shiodome side), 5 minutes; or Shiodome on the Ōedo line.

    Hall 10:00–17:00, last entry 16:45, closed Mondays, free (East Japan Railway Culture Foundation page). Risk: the hall also closes between exhibitions; the current one ends 23 November and the next was not announced on 1 November. The outside of the building can be seen either way.

    From this platform the first train left for Yokohama in 1872, joining the capital to the treaty port and its trade.

    Stage 3 · Steel and electricity

    Perez: Carnegie's Bessemer steel plant, 1875  ·  Japan: arc lamp in Ginza, 1882; the first power station at Kayabachō, 1887; the Yawata steel works, 1901; the Sumida bridges after 1923

    Kachidoki Bridge (勝鬨橋) and the Kachidoki Bridge Museum (かちどき 橋の資料館), Tsukiji 6-20-11, Chūō ward. Nearest stations Tsukiji (Hibiya line, exit 1), Tsukijishijō or Kachidoki (Ōedo line), about 8 minutes.

    Museum Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Saturday; 09:00–16:00 from 1 December to 28 February; free (Tokyo road corporation page). The bridge itself is open at all hours.

    A steel bridge that opened by electric power, built in Japanese steel in 1940, joins the two halves of this revolution in one object.

    Stage 4 · Oil, cars and mass production

    Perez: Ford's Model T, 1908  ·  Japan: Nissan founded 1933; its Yokohama plant, 1934–35; Toyota's first car plant, 1938

    Nissan Yokohama Plant Guest Hall and Engine Museum (日産エンジンミュージアム), Takarachō 2, Kanagawa ward, Yokohama. Nearest station Shin-Koyasu (JR or Keikyū), 17 minutes on foot, or bus 19 to Takarachō.

    Monday to Friday 10:00–16:00, entry by 15:30; closed at weekends and in company holidays; free, no booking for one visitor (Nissan's own page). Nissan had not posted its December list of non-working days on 1 November.

    Nissan built Japanese cars on the American assembly-line model here from 1935, and the building is still inside the working plant.

    Stage 5 · Information

    Perez: Intel's 4004 microprocessor, 1971  ·  Japan: Sony's TR-55 radio, 1955; the Busicom calculator that carried the first 4004, 1971; NEC's PC-8001, 1979

    Akihabara Radio Center (秋葉原ラジオセンター), Soto-Kanda 1-14-2, Chiyoda ward, under the JR viaduct. Nearest station Akihabara, Electric Town exit, 1 minute.

    Free. No operator page found for the building's hours; shops keep their own hours, roughly 10:00 to 19:00 or 20:00. Several stalls have closed since 2023, the latest in March 2026, so expect some shutters.

    Here engineers, students and hobbyists bought the transistors and chips from which Japan's electronics age was built.

    If it rains

    Stage 1. The wall is in the open. In heavy rain look at the east-gate panels from the covered bicycle park and keep the visit short.

    Stage 2. An underground passage runs most of the way from Shimbashi station. Spend the stop inside the hall, or at Tokyo Station under its domes.

    Stage 3. The walk from Shimbashi and the bridge deck are exposed to wind off the bay. Take the Ōedo line one stop from Shiodome to Tsukijishijō and go straight into the museum.

    Stage 4. The museum is indoors. Take the bus both ways to cut the walk to a minute.

    Stage 5. The Radio Center is under the viaduct, a few steps from the covered station exit. Spend the stop inside it and the Radio Kaikan building next door.

    The alternatives

    Stage 1. Gemini's first alternative is Higashi-Shirahige Park and the Shirahige-higashi flats on the Kanebō mill land at Kanegafuchi: a 1.2 km wall of eighteen thirteen-storey blocks, built 1975–82 as a firebreak, with steel fire gates. It is huge, but nothing of the 1889 cotton mill survives, so it shows the site rather than the factory. The second is the Tokyo University of Agriculture and Technology Science Museum at Koganei, full of full-size silk and cotton machines (Thursday 10:00–17:00, free, from Gemini, not checked), about fifty minutes west.

    Stage 2. Tokyo Station's Marunouchi building of 1914, a 335-metre brick front with two domes, is the fallback if the Shimbashi hall is closed; the Jōban train passes through it one stop before Shimbashi. The Ishikawajima shipyard site at Tsukuda fails: only a plaque and a small lighthouse, and its museum opens on Wednesdays and Saturdays only.

    Stage 3. The Kiyosu bridge (1928) and the Eitai bridge (1926), upstream on the Sumida, are both grand steel bridges and open at all hours, near Kiyosumi-Shirakawa and Suitengūmae stations. The stone at Kayabachō marking the first power station of 1887 is only a small marker on a pavement.

    Stage 4. Toyosu Park keeps a dock and a tall yellow crane from the 1939 Ishikawajima shipyard, striking, but the 1950s gas and coal works it stood for are gone under a shopping mall. The Ōta ward industrial plaza and the machine shops of Minami-Kamata show post-war small workshops, not the big plants of the 1930s.

    Stage 5. The NTT Technology History Center at Musashino has room-sized telephone exchanges and early computers, open Thursday and Friday 13:00–17:00, free; it is the better museum, but about 85 minutes from Nissan. The National Museum of Nature and Science in Ueno Park shows the Busicom calculator with the first 4004 chip, in a glass case, beside an early computer; adult entry ¥630 (about $4.01; from Gemini, not checked), a fifteen-minute walk from the flat, so it suits another day.
